title: LEFT JOIN
description: Preserve every chosen left row, explain NULL extension and ON versus WHERE, and count or exclude optional matches without losing identities or multiplying the wrong grain.

questions.question_text: Before later WHERE filters, what does LEFT JOIN preserve from its left input?
options: Every row from the left table appears, regardless of whether a match exists on the right
Left table rows are duplicated for each match
questions.explanation: Each left row participates in matching pairs or a NULL-extended placeholder. Later filters can still remove it, and multiple matches can multiply it.

questions.question_text: In the running example, what does Vikram's department show under LEFT JOIN?
options: NULL, since he has no matching department
questions.explanation: Vikram's row is preserved with NULL filled in for the unmatched department column.

questions.question_text: Does swapping the table order (departments LEFT JOIN employees instead of employees LEFT JOIN departments) produce the same result?
options: No — swapping changes which table's rows are guaranteed to be preserved, producing a fundamentally different query
Only the column order changes, not the rows
questions.explanation: Table order directly determines which side's unmatched rows are kept.

questions.question_text: Which predicate placement can remove unmatched employees when their preservation is required?
options: Using an alias for the tables
Filtering the right table's column in WHERE instead of ON, which discards the very NULL rows LEFT JOIN was meant to preserve
questions.explanation: A null-rejecting right-side WHERE condition, such as d.name=Engineering, removes NULL extension. Not every conceivable right-side WHERE condition does so.

questions.question_text: In a LEFT JOIN, what's the difference between COUNT(d.id) and COUNT(*)?
options: COUNT(d.id) counts nonnull right matches; COUNT(*) counts joined rows including placeholders and multiple pairs
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts result rows, not necessarily distinct left identities when several right matches exist.

questions.question_text: What is the standard way to find rows in the left table with NO match in the right table?
options: LEFT JOIN followed by IS NULL on a right marker guaranteed nonnull in every real match
questions.explanation: A nullable descriptive marker can be NULL on an actual match, so choose a nonnull right identity.

questions.question_text: Is LEFT OUTER JOIN different from LEFT JOIN?
options: No — OUTER is optional; LEFT JOIN and LEFT OUTER JOIN mean the same thing
LEFT OUTER JOIN only works with three or more tables
questions.explanation: The OUTER keyword is optional for LEFT/RIGHT joins, matching how INNER is optional for INNER JOIN.

questions.question_text: Does Marketing (a department with no employees) appear in `employees LEFT JOIN departments`?
options: Yes, once with NULL employee columns
No — LEFT JOIN preserves the LEFT table's (employees') rows, not unmatched right-table rows
This depends on the ON condition only
questions.explanation: Since departments is the right table here, its unmatched rows (like Marketing) are not preserved by a LEFT JOIN.

questions.question_text: Does LEFT JOIN alone guarantee exactly one output row per left row?
options: No, multiple right matches can produce several pairs
Only if left identifiers are integers
questions.explanation: Uniqueness of the match determines whether one-to-many multiplication occurs.

questions.question_text: What does an empty left input produce?
questions.explanation: There are no preserved left rows to extend.

questions.question_text: A left-only condition in ON is false. Must the left row disappear?
options: Yes, ON always filters the preserved input
questions.explanation: ON controls matching; WHERE controls retained result population.

questions.question_text: Which marker is reliable for a no-match test?
options: A right primary key declared nonnull
A CASE label that can be NULL
questions.explanation: A real matched right row cannot have the nonnull marker missing.

questions.question_text: Why can WHERE right_status=confirmed remove unmatched left rows?
options: It automatically creates a foreign key
The NULL-extended comparison is not TRUE
questions.explanation: WHERE retains TRUE and removes FALSE or UNKNOWN.

questions.question_text: Does NULL Engineering information prove an employee has no department at all?
options: No, it can mean no department satisfying that ON filter
questions.explanation: Interpret absence relative to the complete qualifying rule.

questions.question_text: What does COUNT(*) include after a left join?
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts result rows rather than nonnull marker values.

questions.question_text: What reports zero confirmed registrations correctly?
options: COUNT(*) after removing all NULL rows
COUNT(nonnull registration_id) with status eligibility in ON
questions.explanation: The preserved session has no nonnull matched marker when no confirmation qualifies.

questions.question_text: Can a later inner join through an optional right row erase preservation?
options: No, the first LEFT JOIN protects everything
questions.explanation: The entire chain determines final row retention.

questions.question_text: Should DISTINCT hide unexpected pairs before investigating the predicate?
options: No, verify grain and complete matching first
questions.explanation: Unexpected multiplicity can expose an incomplete relationship condition.

questions.question_text: What does departments LEFT JOIN employees preserve?
questions.explanation: Reversing direction changes the report’s guaranteed input population.

questions.question_text: What must explicit output ordering use here?
options: The current physical index order alone
The employee identifier required by the task
questions.explanation: A required ORDER BY states the output contract.

coding_problems.title: Every Employee, Department or Not

original_problem.title: Every Employee, Department or Not
original_problem.description:
Write a query returning `id`, `name` (employee), and `department` for EVERY employee, showing `NULL` for employees with no department, ordered by employee `id`.

```sql
CREATE TABLE departments (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE employees (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  department_id INTEGER,
  manager_id INTEGER,
  salary INTEGER NOT NULL
);
```

**Sample data**:

```sql
INSERT INTO departments (id, name) VALUES (1, 'Engineering'), (2, 'Sales'), (3, 'Marketing');
INSERT INTO employees (id, name, department_id, manager_id, salary) VALUES
(1, 'Asha', 1, NULL, 90000),
(2, 'Rohan', 1, 1, 70000),
(3, 'Neha', 2, 1, 65000),
(4, 'Vikram', NULL, 1, 50000);
```

coding_problems.title: Retain sessions with zero confirmations
coding_problems.task: Return session_id, confirmed_count for every session. Only status confirmed qualifies. Count actual registrations and order by session_id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE sessions(session_id INT PRIMARY KEY); CREATE TABLE registrations(registration_id INT PRIMARY KEY,session_id INT,status VARCHAR(12));
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO sessions VALUES(1),(2),(3); INSERT INTO registrations VALUES(10,1,'confirmed'),(11,1,'cancelled'),(12,1,'confirmed'),(13,2,'cancelled');
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT s.session_id,COUNT(r.registration_id) AS confirmed_count FROM sessions s LEFT JOIN registrations r ON r.session_id=s.session_id AND r.status='confirmed' GROUP BY s.session_id ORDER BY s.session_id;
hints: Use a nonnull right marker inside COUNT.
coding_problems.explanation: The complete ON condition selects qualifying registrations without removing sessions; COUNT of the nonnull registration key returns zero for a null-extended placeholder.

notes:
## Preserve the chosen population even when a relationship is absent

A LEFT JOIN retains each row of its left input through the join operation. When one or more right rows satisfy the ON condition, it returns one result row for each matching pair. When none satisfies that condition, it returns a row with the right-side columns extended by NULL. Later WHERE filters can still remove rows, so preserving the left population requires reasoning about the entire query rather than only spotting the words LEFT JOIN.

Imagine an employee directory where every employee must appear, including someone not assigned to a department. The employees table belongs on the preserved left side. The department label is optional related information, not a reason to erase an employee from the directory. Reversing the inputs instead asks for every department, including departments with no employees. Those are different report requirements, even when they use the same equality relationship.

## Follow the retained employee fixture

The seeded exercise contains Engineering, Sales and Marketing departments. Asha and Rohan belong to Engineering, Neha belongs to Sales, and Vikram has no department identifier. The correct directory has four employee rows. Vikram's department column is NULL. Marketing has no employee and does not appear as an extra row because the report preserves employees rather than all departments.

```sql
SELECT e.id,e.name,d.name AS department
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.id=e.department_id
ORDER BY e.id;
```

The ordered result is Asha/Engineering, Rohan/Engineering, Neha/Sales, and Vikram/NULL. The department key is unique, so each employee finds at most one department. That uniqueness, not the left-join keyword alone, makes the output one row per employee. If a right input contained several qualifying rows per employee, the join would legitimately multiply the employee row into several matching pairs.

A left input with zero rows produces zero result rows even if the right table has data. A nonempty left input with an empty right table produces a NULL-extended row for each left row, subject to later filtering. These boundary cases help distinguish a left join from a full outer join, a Cartesian product or a promise that both entire tables will always be displayed.

## Understand ON as the matching rule

ON determines which right rows count as matches for a particular left row. It can include several key components and eligibility conditions. For a report of each employee's active department information, putting the relevant active condition in ON means an inactive department does not supply a match while the employee can still remain as a NULL-extended row. This is useful when the optional relationship is defined by the complete condition.

A left-side condition in ON does not necessarily remove the left row. If an employee fails that condition, the join can still preserve the employee with no right match. Use WHERE when the requirement is to remove employees from the report population. Confusing population eligibility with match eligibility can produce a query that retains rows the author thought it had excluded.

## Inspect WHERE after null extension

A predicate such as WHERE d.name='Engineering' rejects the NULL-extended rows because the comparison evaluates to UNKNOWN for a missing department. The query may then behave like an inner join for that requirement. This is not an optimizer mistake: WHERE filters the result after the join's logical matching and extension. If the goal is every employee with optional Engineering information, the placement and intended meaning must be reconsidered.

```sql
SELECT e.id,e.name,d.name AS engineering_department
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN departments d
  ON d.id=e.department_id AND d.name='Engineering'
ORDER BY e.id;
```

This form retains all employees while showing an Engineering label only for a qualifying match. It does not mean that Sales employees have no actual department; it means no department satisfying this join's full qualifying rule supplied the optional output. Name the output column and explain NULL in the context of that rule so readers do not confuse missing qualifying evidence with absence of every underlying relationship.

## Use a reliable marker for absence

To find employees with no matching department, use a right-side column that cannot be NULL in a real match, such as the department primary key. After the left join, WHERE d.id IS NULL identifies null extension. Testing a nullable descriptive column can incorrectly classify a matched row whose description happens to be missing. The marker must reflect the schema's nullability guarantee.

```sql
SELECT e.id,e.name
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.id=e.department_id
WHERE d.id IS NULL
ORDER BY e.id;
```

For the stated fixture, this returns Vikram. Depending on foreign-key enforcement, the same query could also identify a nonnull department identifier with no existing parent. Do not assume the only possible absence is a NULL foreign key unless the actual schema proves it. NOT EXISTS can state the same absence question directly when its correlation and eligibility predicates match the intended join condition.

## Count matches rather than placeholders

COUNT(*) counts joined result rows, including a NULL-extended placeholder. COUNT(d.id) counts nonnull matched department identifiers. Grouping a left join can therefore require a nonnull right marker to report zero matches correctly. If there are multiple right matches, COUNT(*) counts their pairs rather than distinct original employees. State the aggregate grain and multiplicity before interpreting the number.

For a department-to-employee report preserving every department, COUNT(e.id) can show zero for Marketing while COUNT(*) would show one placeholder row. That example reverses the preserved population deliberately. It is not the same query as the employee directory, and the two count meanings must not be transferred without checking the direction and cardinality of the actual join.

## Preserve optional facts through later operations

Joining another table after a left join can erase the preserved row if an inner join requires a value from the missing right side. For example, an employee with no department cannot satisfy an ordinary equality inner join through that department's location identifier. If the whole optional chain must remain optional, design and test the chain accordingly instead of assuming the first LEFT JOIN protects every later operation.

Aggregating or applying DISTINCT can also change the output identity. Two employees sharing a name should remain distinct when the directory is one row per employee. Include their stable identifiers rather than collapsing by display name to hide unexpected multiplication. Investigate why extra pairs arise; DISTINCT should express a deliberate result rule rather than cover an incomplete composite-key predicate.

## Test duplicate and missing identities deliberately

Give two employees the same display name while retaining distinct employee identifiers. Both must remain in the directory. Give a workshop two confirmed registration rows with different registration identifiers and verify that both contribute to its count. These fixtures challenge shortcuts that deduplicate names or amounts rather than counting the required relationship facts. A visually repeated row can be a legitimate separate pair, so compare stable identities before calling it a duplicate error.

Also test a missing optional chain on a separate fixture and inspect every predicate after the join. If the query later adds an aggregate or another relation, rerun the unmatched cases. A once-correct left join can lose its intended population when surrounding query logic changes, even while the original ON equality remains untouched.

## Solve two preserved-population tasks

The beginner exercise retains the original directory contract and all seeded exercise identities. Run the original and alternate fixtures, then add an empty employee input and an employee with no department. The result should contain every actual employee exactly once under the unique department key, with NULL where no department matches. Marketing remains absent from this employee-first report unless an employee references it.

For the intermediate exercise, report every workshop session and the number of confirmed registrations. Put the confirmed status test in ON and count the registration primary key. A session with only cancelled registrations must report zero rather than disappear; an empty registration table must give zero for every existing session. Continue with [anti joins](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/anti-join), [join cardinality](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/join-cardinality) and [join predicates](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/join-predicate) to connect preservation with absence, multiplicity and complete matching rules.
